extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in philosophy of mathematics (graduate-level and above)
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedia survey of the metaphysical view called mathematical platonism, its defining theses, main arguments for it (notably the Fregean argument), prominent objections (epistemological and metaphysical), and intermediate/lightweight alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence
rubrics_metrics.description: There are mathematical objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formalized as '∃x Mx' where 'Mx' abbreviates 'x is a mathematical object' true of the objects studied by pure mathematics (numbers, sets, functions). Occurs as one of the three conjuncts defining mathematical platonism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstractness
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical objects are abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An object is abstract iff it is non-spatiotemporal and (therefore) causally inefficacious. Considerations: relatively uncontroversial among philosophers; challenges concern impure sets or contested kinds of numbers (Maddy, Bigelow).

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical objects are independent of intelligent agents and their language, thought, and practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initially left schematic. Natural gloss: counterfactual conditional that had there not been intelligent agents (or had their language, thought, or practices been different), mathematical objects would still exist. The text discusses subtler readings (Counterfactual Independence vs Robust Independence) and worries that simple glosses may not capture intended metaphysical strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical Platonism (threefold definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Platonism = Existence ∧ Abstractness ∧ Independence (i.e., there are abstract mathematical objects independent of us).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central definitional rubric of the article. The entry stresses that platonism in this sense is a metaphysical claim distinct from historical Plato and from added epistemological claims sometimes historically associated with platonism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Object realism
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist abstract mathematical objects (conjunction of Existence and Abstractness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weaker than full platonism because it omits Independence. Object realism allows for mathematical objects that might be dependent on or constituted by humans (e.g., some forms of intuitionism). Philosophical consequences are weaker than platonism's; physicalists may accept dependent non-physical objects (corporations, laws, poems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth-value realism
rubrics_metrics.description: Every well-formed mathematical statement has a unique and objective truth-value independent of our knowledge or current theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphysical claim about truth-values; does not by itself entail existence of mathematical objects. Many nominalists may endorse truth-value realism for basic mathematics. Debates about shifting the discussion from platonism to truth-value realism (Dummett) are noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working realism (methodological realism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics should be practiced 'as if' platonism were true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implies acceptance of certain mathematical methods: (i) classical first-order (or stronger) languages with referring singular terms and quantifiers; (ii) classical rather than intuitionistic logic; (iii) non-constructive methods and axioms (e.g., Axiom of Choice); (iv) impredicative definitions; (v) 'Hilbertian optimism' that every mathematical problem is in principle solvable. Working realism is a methodological stance distinct from metaphysical platonism, though platonism can support it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical Semantics
rubrics_metrics.description: The singular terms of the language of mathematics purport to refer to mathematical objects, and its first-order quantifiers purport to range over such objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A hermeneutic/descriptive claim about mathematical language; 'purport' means that for a sentence to be true it must succeed in referring/ranging as it purports. The premise enjoys prima facie plausibility because mathematical language appears semantically like ordinary language (examples: 'Evelyn is prim.' vs 'Eleven is prime.'). Challenges by nominalists and semantic critics require substantial linguistic/semantic arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth (premise for Fregean argument)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most sentences accepted as mathematical theorems are true (regardless of syntactic/semantic structure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defended in various ways: (a) appeal to logicism (theorems provable from logic and definitions); (b) Quine-Putnam indispensability argument (mathematics indispensable to empirical science, hence likely true); (c) mathematical naturalism (appeal to mathematicians' acceptance and domain-specific standards—claims (2)-(4) in text). Fictionalists resist the naturalistic move.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fregean argument for existence (template)
rubrics_metrics.description: From Classical Semantics + Truth it follows that there must be mathematical objects (Existence): if mathematical sentences purport to refer and are true, then the singular terms must succeed in referring to mathematical objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Template abstracts from Frege's specific logicist commitments. The article treats this as the central argument for mathematical objects and discusses defenses and challenges to its premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quine's Criterion (ontological commitment)
rubrics_metrics.description: A first-order sentence (or set of sentences) is ontologically committed to such objects as must be assumed to be in the range of the variables for the sentence(s) to be true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to argue many mathematical sentences are ontologically committed to mathematical objects if Classical Semantics holds. Criterion is treated as a (standard) definition but has been challenged by philosophers proposing alternative conceptions of ontological commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterfactual Independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Had there not been any intelligent agents, or had their language, thought, or practices been suitably different, there would still have been mathematical objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A common gloss on Independence accepted by many analytic philosophers. The article notes that if Independence is read merely this way, object realism plus this counterfactual seems to imply platonism; but the sufficiency of this gloss to capture platonism's intended content is questioned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robust Independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical objects are metaphysically on a par with ordinary physical objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stronger than Counterfactual Independence: intended to sustain the full analogy between numbers/sets and physical objects (same kind of metaphysical status). Lightweight views reject this stronger thesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benacerraf-style epistemological objection (Field's version)
rubrics_metrics.description: If mathematicians are reliable in accepting true mathematical sentences and any justification of that reliability must be in principle explainable, then if platonism is true this reliability cannot be explained; hence platonism undercuts our justification for mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as three premises: (1) mathematicians are reliable (acceptance implies truth for almost every S); (2) reliability must be, in principle, explainable to justify belief; (3) platonism entails such reliability cannot be explained (because platonic entities are causally isolated). Premise (3) is controversial; alternatives to causal explanations exist and critics propose non-causal accounts of epistemic contact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benacerraf metaphysical objection (structuralist challenge)
rubrics_metrics.description: If natural numbers have only structural properties (positions in a structure), then there is no fact of the matter which object (e.g., which set-theoretic representation) is the number 3; hence numbers are not objects in the ordinary sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two controversial steps: (a) defense of structuralism about numbers; (b) claim that there can be no objects with only structural properties. Structuralists reject the second step. The article cites defenders of structuralism and critics who insist numbers have intrinsic ties to cardinalities, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of Nominalism (Goodman)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever two entities have the same basic constituents they are identical (a strengthening of extensionality obtained by replacing membership with its transitive closure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goodman's principle aims to block set/class formation and supports a nominalist program (favoring mereological sums). The article notes Goodman’s defense is widely viewed as unconvincing given the success of set theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plenitudinous (full-blooded) platonism
rubrics_metrics.description: A plenitude principle: any mathematical objects that could exist actually do exist (so every consistent mathematical theory is true of some universe of mathematical objects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocated by Balaguer and in variants by Linsky & Zalta (object theory). Claims to make mathematical knowledge easy if consistency suffices for truth. Criticisms: undermines reference, lacks a precise plenitude principle, or requires privileging some universes (Martin). Object theory offers a comprehension principle guaranteeing plenitude; critics challenge coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lightweight semantic values / non-eliminative reductionism
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical singular terms have abstract semantic values, but the truth of this may obtain in virtue of more basic, non-abstract facts (so reference to abstract objects can be grounded in non-abstract conditions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows acceptance of object realism and Counterfactual Independence without Robust Independence. Example: a direction as semantic value tied to oriented lines; reference truths obtain via more basic facts about lines. Linnebo discusses how such accounts may validate counterfactual independence while producing disanalogies with physical objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potentialism about mathematics / potential infinity
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical objects exist only in a potential manner (e.g., natural numbers are potentially infinite rather than actually infinite).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspired by Aristotle and the iterative conception: no matter how many sets/numbers have been formed, more may be formed. Applied to sets and sometimes to numbers; contrasts with Cantorian actual infinity. Iterative-conception potentialism has contemporary defenders and formalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualified realism / ontological dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical facts/objects are ontologically dependent or grounded in more fundamental, non-mathematical facts (e.g., facts about provability, structural possibilities, or pluralities that instantiate numbers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rosen's 'qualified realism' and related Aristotelian-inspired accounts: arithmetic truths grounded in facts about pluralities or provability. Kit Fine and others argue sets may be ontologically dependent on their elements. These views accept some form of object realism while rejecting the platonistic picture of independently existing abstract objects.
